frozen_original.title: Trump Pressures Postmaster DeJoy to Slow Mail Delivery Before 2020 Election
frozen_original.synopsis: In mid-2020, Postmaster General Louis DeJoy, a major Trump donor with no postal experience, implemented operational changes to the U.S. Postal Service that slowed mail delivery across the country. The changes included eliminating overtime, removing mail sorting machines, and reducing delivery trips — all in the lead-up to a historic mail-in ballot election during the COVID-19 pandemic. Congressional Democrats and election officials accused the changes of being deliberate voter suppression to benefit Trump. DeJoy was forced to pause some changes under court order. Trump explicitly stated he was opposing postal funding because he didn't want to make it easier for mail-in voting, directly linking postal sabotage to election strategy.

primary.title: Trump Opposed Postal Funding While Linking It to Mail Voting
primary.description_short: Trump opposed additional Postal Service funding in August 2020 and said it was needed to process ballots for universal mail voting.
primary.description_medium: In August 2020, Donald Trump opposed additional Postal Service funding during COVID-19 relief negotiations and said the money was needed to process ballots for universal mail voting. CNBC reported the remarks and quoted Postmaster General Louis DeJoy rejecting the idea that he would make Postal Service decisions at Trump’s direction. The reporting does not substantiate the original claim that Trump pressured DeJoy to slow delivery.
primary.description_long: On August 13, 2020, President Donald Trump opposed additional funding for the U.S. Postal Service during negotiations over coronavirus relief. In a Fox Business interview, he said the Postal Service needed money to process “all of these millions and millions of ballots” and said that without a deal it could not have universal mail-in voting. CNBC reported those remarks and quoted Postmaster General Louis DeJoy saying the idea that he would make Postal Service decisions at Trump’s direction was “wholly off-base.” The reporting supports Trump’s public funding position and the connection he expressly made between postal resources and mail voting. It does not establish that Trump personally directed DeJoy to slow mail delivery. The supplied research notes also distinguish Trump’s opposition to funding from DeJoy’s separate operational changes and report that Trump said he did not know what DeJoy was doing. This record should describe the funding dispute and statement, not assert an unproven instruction to reduce delivery service, voter-suppression intent, or resulting postal harm. No enacted funding decision or measured effect is established by the cited article.
primary.date_precision: day; CNBC publication date and interview remarks are August 13, 2020.
primary.subcategory: Postal Service funding and mail voting

frozen_original.title: Trump Threatens Columbia University Funding Over Gaza Protests
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, the Trump administration threatened to cut $400 million in federal funding to Columbia University over the university's handling of pro-Palestinian protests on campus in 2024, demanding that Columbia adopt new disciplinary policies, restructure its Middle East studies department under federal oversight, and report student protesters to law enforcement. The demands were accompanied by explicit threats of criminal prosecution of university administrators. Columbia's board and interim president faced intense pressure from both the administration and donors. Legal experts called the demands an unconstitutional federal takeover of a private university's internal affairs. The episode was part of a coordinated campaign targeting elite universities the administration accused of harboring antisemitism and radical ideology.

primary.disposition_rationale: After comparing supplied similar records, the March 7 $400 million cancellation is already proposed as a separate child under entry-5752. This card retains the distinct, source-supported March 13 conditions letter as the single unique event and avoids a duplicate cancellation card; no second event is invented.
primary.title: Federal task force sends Columbia nine preconditions for funding negotiations
primary.description_short: A federal task force's March 13 letter set nine preconditions for formal negotiations over restoring Columbia University's canceled federal grants and contracts.
primary.description_medium: On March 13, 2025, the federal Joint Task Force to Combat Antisemitism sent Columbia University a letter listing nine preconditions for formal negotiations to restore canceled federal grants and contracts, according to a March 24 release by HHS, Education and GSA. This repair covers the later letter only. It excludes the March 7 cancellation, already proposed as a separate event in supplied entry-5752, and does not retain unsupported claims of threats of criminal prosecution.
primary.description_long: On March 13, 2025, the federal Joint Task Force to Combat Antisemitism sent Columbia University a letter setting out nine preconditions for formal negotiations to restore canceled federal grants and contracts, according to a March 24 joint release by HHS, Education and GSA. The government statement said Columbia committed to changes involving admissions review, protest and masking rules, immigration-law compliance, regional-studies programs beginning with Middle East and Israel, discipline for Hamilton Hall and encampment cases, the structure of its judicial board, campus security powers, and its Tel Aviv center. This card describes the letter's stated terms and the administration's use of funding restoration as leverage. It does not claim that every requested change was implemented, that the conditions had legal force beyond the funding relationship, or that criminal prosecution was threatened as part of this letter; the frozen entry's prosecution claim is not supported by the reviewed source. The March 7 announcement canceling about $400 million is a separately dated event already proposed in supplied entry-5752, so it is excluded here to avoid duplicate event coverage.
primary.date_precision: Specific date stated in the March 24 GSA release.
primary.subcategory: Federal funding pressure on university governance
organization_tags: Joint Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

source_fact_map.fact: The March 13 letter set nine preconditions for formal negotiations to restore canceled federal grants and contracts.
source_fact_map.quote: March 13th letter detailing 9 preconditions for formal negotiations to restore canceled federal grants and contracts
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Today, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), Department of Education (ED), and the U.S. General Services Administration (GSA) welcomed the statement by Columbia University outlining actions the university is taking in response to the Joint Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism’s March 13th letter detailing 9 preconditions for formal negotiations to restore canceled federal grants and contracts.

source_fact_map.fact: The list of Columbia commitments included review of regional-studies programs beginning with Middle East and Israel.
source_fact_map.quote: Reviewing the portfolio of regional studies programs, starting immediately with those that teach about the Middle East and Israel.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
Columbia has committed to:

- Reviewing admissions procedures to ensure an unbiased admissions process and specifically studying the decline in admissions of Jewish students.
- Clarifying time, place, and manner restrictions to clearly state that protests in academic buildings, and other places necessary for the conduct of university activities, are unacceptable.
- Enforcing a strict anti-masking policy that includes appropriate enforcement mechanisms for violations, including removal from campus or detention for trespassing.
- Adhering to all student visa and immigration laws in cooperation with the Department of Homeland Security.
- Reviewing the portfolio of regional studies programs, starting immediately with those that teach about the Middle East and Israel.
- Enforcing existing disciplinary policies and completing disciplinary proceedings, with meaningful consequences, for Hamilton Hall and encampments.
- Placing the University Judicial Board (UJB) under the Office of the Provost and limiting panel membership to faculty and administrators only.
- Expanding the number of Columbia security personnel and granting them the ability to arrest and remove agitators who foster an unsafe or hostile work or study environment, or otherwise interfere with classroom instruction or the functioning of the university.
- Advance Columbia’s Tel Aviv Center. Programming for the Columbia Tel Aviv Global Hub will launch in Q2 2025.

evidence_map.source_excerpt:
Columbia has committed to:

- Reviewing admissions procedures to ensure an unbiased admissions process and specifically studying the decline in admissions of Jewish students.
- Clarifying time, place, and manner restrictions to clearly state that protests in academic buildings, and other places necessary for the conduct of university activities, are unacceptable.
- Enforcing a strict anti-masking policy that includes appropriate enforcement mechanisms for violations, including removal from campus or detention for trespassing.
- Adhering to all student visa and immigration laws in cooperation with the Department of Homeland Security.
- Reviewing the portfolio of regional studies programs, starting immediately with those that teach about the Middle East and Israel.

- Placing the University Judicial Board (UJB) under the Office of the Provost and limiting panel membership to faculty and administrators only.
- Expanding the number of Columbia security personnel and granting them the ability to arrest and remove agitators who foster an unsafe or hostile work or study environment, or otherwise interfere with classroom instruction or the functioning of the university.
- Advance Columbia’s Tel Aviv Center. Programming for the Columbia Tel Aviv Global Hub will launch in Q2 2025.

frozen_original.title: Trump administration shares immigrant data with foreign governments
frozen_original.synopsis: The Trump administration shared sensitive data on immigrants and asylum seekers with foreign governments, potentially exposing individuals to persecution and endangering those who fled repressive regimes. The data sharing arrangements bypassed standard privacy protections and refugee confidentiality rules, providing detailed personal information including home addresses, family members, and reasons for fleeing to governments that had persecuted the asylum seekers. Human rights organizations reported multiple cases of individuals being targeted by foreign governments using information shared by the Trump administration.

primary.title: Lawsuit Alleges ICE Shared Iranian Asylum Seekers’ Immigration Files with Iran
primary.description_short: A 2026 lawsuit alleges that U.S. officials shared Iranian asylum seekers’ confidential immigration files with Iran beginning in March 2025; DHS denies it.
primary.description_medium: A July 2026 complaint by the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund alleges that the Trump administration adopted a policy in March 2025 to give Iran confidential immigration-file information about Iranian asylum seekers. The complaint says ICE and Iranian officials held monthly meetings to share records. CNN reported the suit and quoted a DHS spokesperson denying the allegation. These are allegations, not court findings; the complaint seeks declaratory and injunctive relief.
primary.description_long: On July 7, 2026, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund filed a complaint in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia through Public Citizen. The complaint alleges that the Trump administration adopted a policy in March 2025 to provide the Iranian government with confidential immigration-file information about Iranians seeking asylum in the United States. It says ICE and Iranian officials held monthly meetings to share records of people in ICE custody and that officials also sent or hand-delivered files. The complaint alleges that hundreds of Iranian detainees seeking asylum were affected and argues that disclosure could endanger applicants and relatives; those claims have not been adjudicated. CNN reported the complaint and quoted a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson saying the allegations that ICE shared asylum application records with Iran were false. The complaint asks the court for declaratory and injunctive relief, so no finding of unlawful sharing or resulting persecution is established here. The evidence is limited to Iranian asylum seekers and the Iranian government. The supplied date of March 1 is only a month-level anchor: the complaint says March 2025, not a specific day. The broader frozen claim about sharing detailed information with multiple foreign governments and documented targeting cases is not supported by these sources and is excluded.
primary.date_precision: month; the complaint identifies March 2025 but not a day, and 2025-03-01 is an anchor only

In addition, since the March 2025 meeting, U.S. government officials have periodically mailed or hand delivered immigration files of Iranians in ICE custody to the Iranian Government.

Jul 7, 2026

PUBLISHED Jul 7, 2026, 6:22 PM ET

A newly filed lawsuit alleges that the Trump administration shared confidential information with Tehran about Iranian asylum seekers as it worked to deport them from the United States.

According to the lawsuit, filed Tuesday in the US District Court of the District of Columbia, many Iranian asylum seekers in the US are pro-democracy protestors, members of religious minorities, or members of the LGBTQ community.

It was filed by Public Citizen on behalf of the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund.
